title: Removable prosthesis
description: Problems caused by or related to complete and partial dentures — tissue injury, retention loss, occlusal errors, and structural failure.

problems.description: Rolls of excess soft tissue build up in the sulcus where the denture flange sits, often painless but the denture stops fitting around the tissue folds.
problems.conditionName: Denture irritation hyperplasia (denture-induced hyperplasia / epulis fissuratum)
problems.etiology:
Repeated low-grade trauma from an overextended or ill-fitting denture flange — especially as the underlying ridge resorbs away and leaves the flange digging into the sulcus mucosa. The tissue responds to that chronic mechanical insult with fibrous hyperplastic proliferation [1]. The longer an old, ill-fitting denture is worn without review, the worse this gets [2].

The mechanism is not inflammatory in the classical sense. Histologically the lesion looks like a fibroepithelial polyp: dense collagenous fibrous tissue lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium [1]. There's no infection involved unless ulceration opens the door to secondary organisms.
problems.presentation:
What you see:

- **Soft tissue rolls or folds** in the sulcus, almost always at the labial or buccal flange margins of an old complete or partial denture [1].
- The tissue is folded over the denture flange edge — one fold labial, one lingual/palatal, with the flange sitting between them.
- Usually **asymptomatic** unless there's ulceration at the base of the fold, in which case the patient reports a dull ache or soreness.
- Very common in the anterior maxillary sulcus region, where ridge resorption is greatest.
problems.results:
- Clinical diagnosis: the fold of tissue precisely corresponds to the flange border — it's the mirror image of the flange extension.
- Palpation: firmer than normal mucosa, non-fluctuant, non-blanching.
- No significant cervical lymphadenopathy.
- Denture assessment will confirm over-extension or poor fit of the offending flange [2].
- **Biopsy** is not always necessary but confirms fibroepithelial polyp histology if there's any doubt [1]. Always send excised tissue for histology.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The location is the giveaway: the folds sit precisely at the margin of the denture flange, not away from it. That spatial relationship — tissue fold wrapping the flange edge — is the defining picture.

Contrast with:

- **Fibroepithelial polyp elsewhere in the mouth**: same histology, but not in the sulcus at the flange border.
- **Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate**: sits on the palate under the fitting surface, not at the flange margin; associated with Candida and poor denture hygiene — belongs to the palate origin.
- **Denture stomatitis**: palatal redness under the upper denture, not sulcus rolls — palate origin.
problems.treatment:
Two steps: excise the tissue, then fix the denture [1].

**Surgical:**

- Complete excision of the hyperplastic tissue, usually under local anaesthetic [1].
- Temporary removal of the denture for an initial period allows the mucosa to settle and helps define the extent of excision needed.
- Pre-prosthetic considerations apply — excision may need to precede new denture construction.
- Send all excised tissue for histological examination.

**Prosthetic:**

- The ill-fitting denture must then be replaced or relined. Excision without addressing the denture means the tissue simply regrows [2].
- If the flange is over-extended, shorten it; if the denture base is grossly ill-fitting, reline or replace [2].
problems.prognosis: With complete excision and denture correction, resolution is good and recurrence is uncommon if the new denture fits properly [1]. Without fixing the denture, recurrence is predictable — the same mechanical trigger is still present. The condition itself carries no malignant potential; histology is benign fibrous tissue.

citations.quote: This is a very common hyperplastic response to repeated trauma, e.g. following denture-induced ulceration. Classically, seen as rolls of tissue in the sulcus related to a denture flange. Histology is similar to a fibroepithelial polyp. Rx: complete excision with temporary removal of dentures allows healing. Consider simple pre-prosthetic measures and replace F/F.

As a result of resorption all dentures become progressively ill-fitting, → loss of retention and stability. Movement of dentures in function may result in: Resorption. Predisposition to candidal infection. Denture irritation hyperplasia (…… Problems in denture wearers, p. 426). Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate.

problems.description: A sharply defined painful ulcer appears under or at the edge of a denture, usually within days of fitting or after a change to the denture.
problems.etiology:
A sharp ridge, roughness on the fitting surface, an over-extended flange, or an occlusal premature contact creates a focal point of pressure or friction against the underlying mucosa. That mechanical insult breaches the epithelium, producing an ulcer [1].

The reason occlusal faults matter here: a premature occlusal contact displaces the denture laterally or anteriorly during function, so the flange edge scrapes against a different part of the mucosa with each chew. This means the sore spot may not coincide with any obvious roughness on the fitting surface — the ulcer is caused by repeated displacement, not a single contact point [1].
problems.presentation:
- Patient reports a sore spot under or at the edge of a new or recently adjusted denture, often appearing within the first 24–48 hours of wear.
- The ulcer is **well-defined, single**, with a yellowish slough base and an erythematous halo — consistent with a mechanical rather than aphthous origin.
- Location corresponds to the point of pressure: the lingual or lateral ridge for a displaced denture, the flange margin for an over-extension, the crest for a fitting-surface flaw [1].
- Pain worse during eating or when the denture is worn; relieves when the denture is removed.
problems.results:
- **Pressure relief paste** (e.g. pressure indicator paste or Fit-Checker) painted onto the fitting surface reveals focal high-pressure areas when the denture is seated [1].
- Systematic examination of fitting and occlusal surfaces identifies the cause.
- If pain moves to a different site after each adjustment, think occlusal displacement rather than fitting-surface roughness [1].
- Ulcer resolves once the denture is not worn for 24–48 h, which confirms the traumatic origin.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The most useful clinical clue is the **spatial relationship between the ulcer and the denture**. The ulcer sits precisely where the denture contacts the mucosa under load.

Compare to:

- **Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS)**: ulcers at non-contact sites, round, recurrent, no temporal link to denture wear, often on non-keratinized mucosa.
- **Traumatic ulcer under a denture suggesting malignancy**: any ulcer that persists beyond 2–3 weeks after removing the cause needs biopsy — the rule applies equally to denture wearers [2].
- **Denture stomatitis**: diffuse palatal redness, not a focal ulcer.
problems.treatment:
- Patient should **continue wearing the denture** if at all possible and return as soon as possible so the affected area can be identified and adjusted [3].
- If that's not practical: stop wearing the denture until 24 hours before the next appointment, so the tissue mark is still visible [3].
- Use pressure indicator paste to localize the fault, then relieve the fitting surface at that point [1].
- Smooth any roughness and reduce any over-extension [4].
- Check occlusion: if occlusal faults are causing displacement, adjust the occlusion — relieving the fitting surface alone will just move the ulcer [1].
- Tissue conditioners applied to the fitting surface allow gradual, even pressure redistribution and are particularly useful where multiple sore areas exist or the tissues are already traumatized [4].
problems.prognosis: With cause identified and corrected, traumatic ulcers heal within 1–2 weeks. Without adjustment, they persist and can progress to larger mucosal erosions. Any ulcer that has not healed within 2–3 weeks after removing the cause must be biopsied.

citations.quote: This can be due to a variety of causes, including roughness of the fitting surface, errors in the occlusion, lack of FWS, a bruxing habit, a retained root, or other pathology. Forward or lateral displacement of a denture due to a premature contact can lead to inflammation of the ridge on the lingual or lateral aspect, respectively. With continued resorption, bony ridges become prominent and the mental foramina is exposed, which can lead to localized areas of specific pain.
Under a denture or other appliance suggests traumatic ulceration.

If pain is experienced, the patient should try to continue wearing their dentures and return for adjustment as soon as possible so that affected areas can easily be seen. If this is not possible, they should stop wearing the dentures until 24h prior to the next visit.

These are r0esilient materials which give a more even distribution of loading and thus promote tissue recovery. They are particularly useful where ill-fitting dentures have caused trauma, as it is important to allow the tissues to recover before impressions for replacement dentures or a rebase are taken.

problems.description: A previously adequate complete denture becomes loose and dislodges in function, even though the patient has been managing fine for years.
problems.conditionName: Loss of denture retention due to ridge resorption (ill-fitting complete denture)
problems.etiology:
Resorption of the alveolar ridge is progressive and irreversible after extraction. The ridge gets smaller over years and the denture fitting surface — cast from an earlier ridge shape — no longer matches the tissue [1]. The peripheral seal that creates suction for the upper denture breaks down as the flanges lose contact with the sulcus walls.

For the lower denture, the problem is worse: the mandible resorbs more quickly than the maxilla, so the lower arch becomes even flatter, giving less surface area and less muscle-groove retention [2].

A fixed post-dam that was added without seating the denture correctly can compound the problem — if it prevents the denture from seating fully, it reduces the mucosal contact that retention depends on [3].
problems.presentation:
- Patient reports the denture has gradually become looser over months to years.
- The upper denture drops during eating or speaking; the lower denture lifts and rocks.
- Distinction between **static** and **functional** retention matters: a denture may feel retained when the patient opens and closes gently (static retention) but dislodge the moment it takes any lateral or anterior occlusal load (functional retention) [4].
- Often accompanied by ridge soreness, as the now-mobile denture scrapes the mucosa during function.
problems.results:
- Clinical test: seat the denture, apply gentle traction on the lower border — upper denture should resist vertical displacement. If it drops with minimal force, the fitting surface is no longer adapting.
- Check the post-dam: if it prevents full seating, the mucosal contact is compromised [3].
- Palpate the ridge: a fibrous, mobile anterior maxillary ridge feels boggy and displaces under finger pressure — it cannot provide stable support [5].
- OVD assessment: check the freeway space — if the existing denture has caused tooth surface wear, the OVD may have reduced, affecting occlusal balance and denture stability.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key clinical distinction is **static versus functional retention** [4]. A denture with poor static retention is loose at rest. A denture with poor functional retention is retained when the patient is still but displaces the moment the muscles and occlusion act on it — and this is the more common clinical presentation with a flabby or resorbed ridge.

Contrast:

- **Poor static retention**: fitting surface doesn't conform, no peripheral seal, denture drops even at rest.
- **Poor functional retention**: fitting surface adequate at rest but occlusal forces or jaw movements break the seal in function — overerupted opposing teeth are a classic cause [5].
problems.treatment:
Options depend on severity [2]:

- **Relining or rebasing**: where only the fitting surface needs improvement. The material of choice for a permanent reline is heat-cure acrylic. Self-cure chairside relines are inferior and interim only [6].
- **Tissue conditioner** first if the mucosa is traumatized: allows recovery before definitive impressions are taken [4].
- **Replacement denture**: when OVD, tooth position, and fit all need attention. For older patients, a copy technique minimizes adaptation burden [7].
- For the **flabby anterior maxillary ridge**: mucostatic impressions with an open anterior window special tray — the aim is to record the ridge without displacing it, because displacing it during impression-taking leads to instability and soreness in the finished denture [5].
- **Implant-retained overdenture**: gold standard for the severely resorbed lower ridge; two implants at canine positions provide retention and dramatically improve function [2].
problems.prognosis: Well-made replacement dentures restore function in most patients. The mandible resorbs more quickly than the maxilla, so the lower denture will eventually become loose again — resorption is progressive [2]. Implant retention arrests the functional problem but not the resorption.

citations.quote: As a result of resorption all dentures become progressively ill-fitting, → loss of retention and stability. Movement of dentures in function may result in: Resorption. Predisposition to candidal infection. Denture irritation hyperplasia.

Resorption is progressive with time, which is a good argument for avoiding rendering young patients edentulous. The mandible resorbs more quickly than the maxilla, which exacerbates the problem of retention for −/F. Management is dependent upon the severity of the problem and the patient's biological age.

If your previous colleague had overbuilt the post-dam in acrylic, it would prevent the denture from seating properly, thus reducing overall mucosal contact. Close mucosal contact and an adequate saliva flow are vital for retention.
Is the static or functional retention of the upper complete denture poor?

There appears to be an anterior maxillary fibrous, 'flabby' ridge, and the lower anterior teeth have overerupted somewhat over time. The fibrous ridge will affect the support of the upper denture, and as a result of the occlusal force anteriorly with the overerupted anterior teeth, this will tend to break the posterior border seal of the maxillary plate.

Rebasing is indicated where the only feature of F/F that requires improvement is the fitting surface; otherwise consider replacement F/F using the copy method. For rebasing, the material of choice is heat-cure acrylic, but this necessitates the patient being without their dentures while the addition is being made. Self-cure acrylic applied at the chair-side appears attractive, but its properties are inferior.

Successful function with complete dentures depends to a marked degree upon the patient's ability to control them. This ability is learnt during a period of denture use. When replacement dentures become necessary, it is helpful if the new appliances require as little adaptation as possible to the existing skills. This is generally considered to be particularly important for the older patient.

problems.description: The patient complains of general soreness throughout the mouth under new dentures, sore jaw muscles, and clicking teeth when speaking — not a single focal ulcer.
problems.conditionName: Increased occlusal vertical dimension (OVD error — overclosed or over-opened denture)
problems.etiology:
When a complete denture is made with too great an occlusal vertical dimension, the patient's muscles of mastication are forced to work from a position of extension rather than from the physiological rest position. The freeway space — normally 2–4 mm — is eliminated or reversed [1]. The result is continuous muscle strain because the elevator muscles cannot relax into the rest position between chewing cycles.

At the other extreme, too little OVD (overclosured) collapses the lower face height, drives the corners of the mouth into a fold that traps moisture, and may set up angular cheilitis as a downstream consequence [2]. Most denture problems of this type occur because the OVD was set incorrectly at the wax-rim stage or because the patient's natural freeway space was not assessed properly [1].
problems.presentation:
Excess OVD:

- Generalized soreness across the whole denture-bearing area, not localized.
- Teeth click together during speech — the 'S' sound is affected by altered freeway space [3].
- Jaw muscle fatigue and aching, worse with sustained wearing.
- Patient notices the upper and lower teeth seem to contact constantly.

Reduced OVD (overclosure):

- Face looks 'sunken' or 'collapsed' at the lower third.
- Angular cheilitis at the corners of the mouth.
- The patient may report that chewing feels oddly effortful.
- Tongue-biting and cheek-biting are more common.
problems.results:
- **Freeway space assessment**: patient in rest position, Frankfort plane horizontal. Measure rest face height and then denture face height [1]. Normal FWS is 2–4 mm. If OVD = rest face height, FWS is zero.
- **Phonetic check**: ask the patient to say 'sixty-six' or 'Mississippi' — the 'S' sound requires teeth to approach but not quite contact. If they click, OVD is too high [3].
- **Facial profile**: photographically compare to pre-extraction records if available.
- No specific radiographic finding, but DPT confirms condylar position is not contributing.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing about OVD problems: they cause **generalized** soreness, not a focal ulcer. Every part of the denture-bearing area is affected because every part of the mucosa is under continuous load. A fitting surface problem causes a single sore spot; an OVD problem causes burning across the whole arch [4].

An increased OVD is a commonly missed cause of generalized soreness — clinicians tend to look for fitting surface flaws and keep adjusting them while the occlusal cause goes untouched. If pain moves each time an adjustment is made, the occlusion is the culprit [4].
problems.treatment:
- The OVD cannot be corrected by adjusting the fitting surface — the jaw relationship has to be re-recorded [4].
- Mild excess OVD: selective grinding of the occlusal surfaces to restore freeway space. Only safe if the OVD is slightly increased; grinding away too much destroys the occlusion.
- Gross error: new dentures with a correctly established jaw relationship.
- **No patient should be expected to become accustomed to a denture with an increased vertical dimension** [5] — this is not an adaptation problem, it is a prescription error.
- For borderline cases, occlusal pivots (wax additions to existing dentures) can trial a change in OVD before committing to new dentures [6].
problems.prognosis: Correcting the OVD resolves muscle soreness and tissue inflammation reliably. The longer the incorrect OVD has been in place, the more mucosal trauma has accumulated and the longer the tissue needs to recover after correction.

citations.quote: The FWS is the space between the occlusal surfaces of the teeth when the mandible is in the rest position. In the majority of patients it is 2–4mm. The OVD for an edentulous patient can therefore be determined by measuring their resting face height and subtracting a FWS.

Burning mouth: This can be due to (i) local causes, e.g. ↑ OVD or sensitivity to acrylic monomer, or be unrelated to the denture (e.g. irritant mouth washes, candidiasis); or (ii) systemic causes, e.g. the menopause, deficiency states, cancerophobia, or xerostomia.
Together in mouth. Examine vertical dimension, occlusion, aesthetics, and phonetics ('S' sound will be affected by ↑ or ↓ FWS).

If there is no obvious cause relating to the fitting surface remember that occlusal faults can cause displacement and mucosal trauma, and an excessive OVD is a common cause of generalized soreness under −/F.
However, no patient should be expected to become accustomed to a denture with an increased vertical dimension.
The effect of an ↑ in OVD can be assessed by self-cure addition to the existing dentures (occlusal pivots), but remember that this irreversibly alters them.

problems.description: A complete denture cracks or breaks, often in the midline, without any obvious single trauma event.
problems.etiology:
Most midline fractures are not caused by dropping the denture — they happen in the mouth. The mechanism is **fatigue failure of the acrylic under repeated flexion** [1]. Every chewing cycle flexes the base slightly. Over hundreds of thousands of cycles, micro-cracks propagate until the base gives way, usually at the thinnest or most stressed section.

Factors that accelerate fatigue:

- **Flabby ridges**: the soft tissue compresses unevenly under load, flexing the base more with each cycle [1].
- **Palatal tori**: the torus stops the palatal vault flexing, so the stress concentrates at the lateral junction [1].
- **Excessive occlusal forces** or occlusal faults that create uneven loading [1].
- **Notching** of the denture for a prominent fraenum reduces cross-sectional area and creates a stress riser [1].
problems.presentation:
- Patient reports the denture 'just snapped' — usually in two pieces, usually along the midline of the upper denture.
- Sometimes they noticed a hairline crack weeks beforehand that they ignored.
- No single traumatic episode, or the event that broke it was trivially minor (e.g., dropped a short distance into a sink) [2].
- On inspection: the fracture line is often at the midpalatal suture region of an upper denture, perpendicular to the alveolar ridge.
problems.results:
- Examine the fitting surface: flabby ridges, tori, areas of uneven wear.
- Check occlusion: unilateral prematurities or excursive interferences increase asymmetric loading.
- Ask about previous fractures: recurrence confirms the structural cause rather than a single accident.
- Examine for palatal torus under the base — requires relief in the denture, and if not relieved properly, concentrates stress.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The midline location is characteristic for upper dentures and reflects the natural line of greatest flexure across the palate. For lower dentures, fractures tend to occur at the thinnest cross-section near fraenal notches.

Contrast:

- **Accidental fracture from a single drop**: the fracture line is irregular and the patient can describe the exact event.
- **Fatigue fracture**: clean line, midline, history of repeated near-breaks or the current break follows a long wearing history with no single trauma [1].
- If a patient has a **documented history of fractures** of multiple successive dentures, the design needs a structural solution — metal reinforcement — rather than a simple repair [1].
problems.treatment:
- **Repair**: if the denture is otherwise satisfactory, repair with heat-cure acrylic is stronger than cold-cure and should be the default [3]. Cold-cure repair is acceptable as a temporary measure.
- **Address the cause** [1]:
  - Palatal torus: provide adequate relief in the fitting surface so the torus does not create a fulcrum.
  - Flabby ridge: use a mucostatic impression to avoid differential loading.
  - Occlusal faults: remount and equilibrate.
- **Metal base or cast-metal strengthener**: indicated when multiple fractures have occurred or the structural problem cannot be resolved by design alone [1].
- **Avoid notching fraenal relief too deeply**: notches are stress risers. Shallow relief is better than deep notching [1].
problems.prognosis: Repair without addressing the cause leads to re-fracture. If the structural risk factors — torus, flabby ridge, occlusal fault — are corrected, a well-made metal-reinforced or heat-cure acrylic denture should last without further fracture.

citations.quote: Apart from carelessness, this is usually caused by occlusal faults or fatigue of the acrylic due to continual stressing by small forces. Flexing of the denture can occur with flabby ridges, palatal tori, and following resorption. Notching of a denture, e.g. relief for a prominent fraenum, can also predispose to #. Rx depends upon the aetiology, but in some cases provision of a metal plate or a cast-metal strengthener may be necessary.
She is afraid that the denture, fitted 3 years ago, will shortly break in half.
There is a risk of another fracture if the denture has been repaired in cold-cure acrylic.

problems.description: Partial denture wearers develop new caries at the necks of abutment teeth and notice plaque builds up more heavily around the clasp areas.
problems.conditionName: Removable partial denture-related abutment caries and periodontal damage
problems.etiology:
Removable partial dentures increase plaque accumulation and change plaque composition at the teeth they contact [1]. The clasp arms and connectors create stagnation zones: plaque accumulates at the gingival margin of the abutment teeth where metal sits close to the gingival sulcus. The metal also reduces saliva clearance in those zones.

Poor denture design compounds this: a denture that does not sit passively in the rest position, or that has connectors running too close to the gingival margin, creates constant low-grade trauma and creates a protected niche for bacteria [1]. Abutment teeth under excessive clasp tension also sustain periodontal trauma: the crest of the alveolar bone around the abutment is gradually overloaded if the clasp is too tight or the denture rocks around the fulcrum axis [2].
problems.presentation:
- Caries at the cervical margin of abutment teeth, often in areas that are hard to see without removing the denture.
- Gingival inflammation and bleeding around the abutment teeth specifically — rather than a generalized pattern.
- Plaque visible at the gingival margin where clasps sit.
- Sometimes the patient reports the clasp feels loose or is causing pain on the abutment tooth [2].
- In long-standing cases, radiographs show crestal bone loss specifically around the abutment teeth.
problems.results:
- **BPE** around abutment teeth specifically: codes 1–3 are common in P/P wearers; a code 3 or 4 around an abutment tooth that was healthy before denture placement points to prosthesis-related periodontal damage.
- **Vitality testing** of the abutment tooth: excessive clasp tension can cause traumatic occlusion or leverage that eventually leads to pulpitis or loss of vitality [2].
- **Radiograph** of abutment teeth: periapical and bitewing to check for cervical caries and crestal bone level.
- **Denture survey**: check clasp tension, connector position relative to gingival margin, and assess whether the denture is rocking on the abutment teeth.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The pattern matters: **caries and periodontal damage are localized to the abutment teeth**, not distributed across the rest of the dentition. This distinguishes partial denture-related damage from generalized high caries risk.

Contrast:

- **Poor OH causing generalized caries**: affects all susceptible surfaces, not just abutments.
- **Fixed bridge secondary caries**: damage at the bridge margin — but this is in the fixed-prosthesis origin.
- The combination of clasp-adjacent cervical caries plus localized periodontal inflammation specifically under the connector is the fingerprint of partial denture harm [1].
problems.treatment:
- **Denture hygiene instruction**: the fitting surface and clasps must be cleaned daily with soap, water, and a brush [3]. Plaque on the fitting surface is often the patient's biggest blind spot.
- **Redesign or reline** the partial denture: connectors that impinge on the gingival margin should be kept clear; clasps should engage only 0.25 mm of undercut for cobalt–chrome to avoid excessive flexion forces [4].
- **Treat the caries and periodontal disease** as standard: cervical lesions on abutment teeth are often best restored with glass ionomer cement because it releases fluoride and sits in a difficult moisture-control zone.
- If an abutment tooth has been lost due to caries or periodontitis: the denture requires redesign — the support and retention balance has changed.
- **Review frequency**: P/P wearers need more frequent recalls than the edentulous patient, precisely because of this risk [1].
problems.prognosis: Damage is reversible in the early stages with improved hygiene and denture modification. Once abutment teeth are lost, the saddle position changes and denture stability deteriorates — the remaining teeth bear more load, accelerating further loss. Poorly designed RPDs have a cumulative destructive effect over years.

citations.quote: These can be minimally invasive as only minor (or no) tooth preparation is required but ↑ plaque accumulation/changes in composition. Damage to soft tissues and remaining teeth is exacerbated by poor denture design and/or lack of patient care.
Pain from an individual tooth on P/P: Excessive load and/or traumatic occlusion. Leverage due to unstable denture. Clasp arm too tight.

When new dentures are fitted, the importance of regular, thorough cleaning, especially of fitting surfaces, with soap, water, and a brush to prevent the build-up of plaque, stain, and calculus should be emphasized.

Cast (cobalt–chrome) clasps are stiff, easily distorted, and liable to #. However, provided they are limited to undercuts of 0.25mm, the advantage of being able to cast them as an integral part of a denture framework offsets these drawbacks.

problems.description: The palate under a complete upper denture develops a lumpy, nodular surface — dozens of small red-pink papillary projections covering the fitting-surface area.
problems.conditionName: Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate (denture-related)
problems.etiology:
What happens is that prolonged wearing of a complete upper denture — especially night-time wear without removal — creates a warm, low-oxygen microenvironment on the palatal mucosa where Candida thrives [1]. The trauma from a poorly fitting or constantly worn denture adds a mechanical insult on top of the candidal colonisation, and the palatal mucosa responds with papillary hyperplasia: multiple small nodular projections of hyperplastic tissue grow from the fitting-surface area [2].

The link to Candida is not incidental. Denture stomatitis — of which this is a more advanced morphological variant — is caused by Candida albicans in 90% of cases [1]. The reason the palate specifically is affected, rather than the lower ridge, is that the upper denture creates a covered, sealed niche against the palate that traps organisms and prevents salivary clearance.
problems.presentation:
Usually symptomless — the patient is often unaware until the denture is removed and the palate is examined [1]. What you'll see on lifting the denture is a field of small (1–3 mm) red or pink papillary projections covering the fitting-surface area of the palate, with surrounding erythema. In some cases the affected area also shows the diffuse redness of underlying denture stomatitis.

The palate surface feels velvety and granular on palpation, compared with the smooth firm mucosa of a healthy vault. The nodules don't ulcerate unless secondarily traumatized.
problems.results:
Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic distribution of nodules matching the denture footprint [2]. The spatial correspondence between the hyperplastic zone and the fitting-surface area of the denture is the key finding.

Swab or smear of the palate for Candida is helpful to confirm active candidosis and guide antifungal choice. No radiographic investigation is needed.

In cases where nodules are unusually large, asymmetric, or located outside the obvious denture footprint, biopsy is appropriate — though true malignant transformation of inflammatory papillary hyperplasia is not described.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The defining feature is the carpet of small papillary projections strictly confined to the fitting-surface zone of the palate under the upper denture — the nodules don't extend to the non-covered palate or soft tissue elsewhere [2]. That restricted distribution separates it from other mucosal conditions.

Contrast:
- **Denture stomatitis (Newton type I and II)**: erythema and petechiae under the denture, but the surface is flat or granular rather than genuinely papillary and nodular. Papillary hyperplasia is the Newton type III presentation — a more advanced, structural change.
- **Denture irritation hyperplasia (epulis fissuratum)**: rolls of fibrous tissue at the denture flange margin in the sulcus, not on the palatal fitting surface.
- **Erythematous candidosis from antibiotics/steroid inhaler**: diffuse palatal redness without nodularity and without the denture footprint pattern.
problems.treatment:
The goal is to eliminate the Candida, remove the denture at night, and then deal with the residual hyperplastic tissue if it doesn't resolve [2].

- **Remove dentures at night.** Night-time wear is a primary driver — this is the most important single instruction [1].
- **Denture hygiene**: brush fitting surface and soak in hypochlorite cleanser daily [1]. The denture acts as a reservoir for Candida and must be treated alongside the mucosa.
- **Antifungal**: miconazole gel applied to the fitting surface before insertion is the mainstay [1]. Systemic fluconazole if topical measures fail [1].
- **Surgical reduction**: if papillary hyperplasia persists after adequate antifungal treatment and improved hygiene, surgical reduction of the hyperplastic nodules is needed before making a new or relined denture [2]. Leaving the irregular tissue in place means any new denture will sit on a poor foundation.
- Replace the denture if it is ill-fitting, to remove the ongoing mechanical stimulus.
problems.prognosis: Antifungal treatment and removal at night will clear the candidosis and often reduce the erythema. The papillary tissue itself, once established, rarely resolves fully without surgical reduction [2]. With tissue reduction and a new well-fitting denture, recurrence is uncommon provided night-time removal and hygiene are maintained.

citations.quote: Also known as denture sore mouth, a misnomer because the condition is usually symptomless. Classically, seen as redness of the palate under a F/− denture, with petechial and whitish areas. 90% of cases due to Candida albicans, 9% to other Candida spp., and <1% to other organisms, e.g. Klebsiella spp.
Coexisting papillary hyperplasia of palate may need surgical reduction.

problems.description: Recession and soft-tissue stripping develop around abutment teeth of a lower acrylic partial denture — the gum pulls away from teeth that were periodontally healthy before the denture was fitted.
problems.conditionName: Gingival stripping by tissue-borne acrylic partial denture (gum-stripper)
problems.etiology:
The problem is a design mismatch. An acrylic partial denture in the lower arch without rests on abutment teeth is a **mucosa-borne** (tissue-borne) denture: it has no direct tooth support, so occlusal loads are transmitted entirely to the mucosa [1]. Under function, the denture sinks into the soft tissue and can displace apically against the gingival margins of the remaining teeth. Repeat loading in this direction strips the gingival tissues away from the cervical area of the abutment tooth — hence the term gum-stripper [1].

This is less a problem in the upper arch because the palatal vault provides broad mucosal support that resists this sinking. In the lower arch there is no comparable vault, so tissue-only support is inherently less stable [2].
problems.presentation:
- Recession affecting the labial or buccal gingivae of teeth adjacent to the denture saddle — specifically those teeth the acrylic base runs close to.
- The patient may report soreness at the gingival margin on the side where the denture base contacts. Alternatively, the recession is painless and noted incidentally at a review appointment.
- On examination: the acrylic connector or base runs across or close to the gingival margin of the natural teeth, with no clearance from the soft tissue.
- Increased plaque accumulation and gingival inflammation at the contact zones, because the acrylic stagnates plaque and blocks self-cleansing.
problems.results:
- Clinical examination with the denture in place: check whether the connector or saddle base runs directly over the gingival margins rather than clearing them [3].
- Measure recession with a graduated probe: recession specifically at teeth adjacent to acrylic connectors or base extensions suggests a mechanical cause.
- BPE of all teeth, comparing scores around abutment teeth to the rest of the dentition — a selective pattern of damage at the denture contact sites points to the prosthesis as the cause.
- Remove the denture and check for tooth mobility: excessive clasp tension or leverage from an unstable denture may compound periodontal damage [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The pattern of recession is the diagnostic clue: it maps precisely to where the acrylic base or connector runs against the gingival margin, rather than being generalised across the arch [3]. What marks this out from other causes of recession:

- **Generalised recession from toothbrush trauma**: uniform, on buccal surfaces across multiple teeth regardless of denture contact.
- **Periodontal disease**: bone loss and pocketing are the primary findings, not just recession at connector sites.
- **Clasping-related damage**: clasp-arm trauma causes cervical caries and periodontal damage at the tooth the clasp engages, not at every connector-contacted surface.

The thing is, this condition is largely preventable by design. When financial constraints make an acrylic base necessary, specific design steps can avoid the gum-stripper outcome: keeping the base clear of gingival margins, avoiding interdental acrylic extensions, and adding wrought stainless steel rests to provide some tooth support [3].
problems.treatment:
- **Modify or replace the denture** to relieve acrylic from gingival margins wherever possible [3]. Where the base cannot avoid the area, reduce the labio-gingival extensions.
- **Add rests** on appropriate abutment teeth to convert the denture from tissue-borne to partially tooth-borne, reducing the sinking force on the mucosa [2].
- **Instruct on denture hygiene**: brushing the fitting surface with soap and water to reduce plaque accumulation against the adjacent gingival margins [5].
- **Periodontal treatment**: root surface debridement and oral hygiene instruction for the affected teeth.
- If recession is significant and function or aesthetics are compromised: consider soft tissue augmentation (connective tissue graft or similar) after the denture has been corrected — surgery without fixing the cause will fail.
- For long-term management: a cobalt–chrome framework denture with correctly designed rests and connectors well clear of the gingival margins is the better solution if the patient can be referred or the practice offers this.
problems.prognosis: Recession caused by a gum-stripper does not self-correct. Removing the cause stops further progression, but the tissue lost does not regenerate without surgical intervention. With design correction and good oral hygiene, the inflammatory component resolves and the rate of loss slows to zero.

citations.quote: Gum-stripper: A tissue-borne partial denture which can 'sink'.
Tissue-only support should be utilized when no suitable teeth are available, and is less damaging in the upper than the lower arch, because of the palatal vault.

However, where financial constraints C/I a metal base, attention to the following may avoid the production of a gum-stripper: Wide mucosal coverage to provide maximum support. Keep base clear of the gingival margins wherever possible. No interdental extensions of acrylic. Point contact and wide embrasures between natural and artificial teeth. Labial flanges for extra retention and bracing. Additional support from wrought SS rests.
Pain from an individual tooth on P/P: Excessive load and/or traumatic occlusion. Leverage due to unstable denture. Clasp arm too tight.

When new dentures are fitted, the importance of regular, thorough cleaning, especially of fitting surfaces, with soap, water, and a brush to prevent the build-up of plaque, stain, and calculus should be emphasized.

problems.description: An elderly patient's longstanding dentures progressively stop fitting — the jaws appear to have grown larger and the patient now has difficulty with extractions that would previously have been routine.
problems.conditionName: Paget's disease of bone — jaw involvement with ill-fitting dentures and BRONJ risk
problems.etiology:
Paget's disease disrupts the normal, orderly cycle of bone remodelling and replaces it with chaotic alternation of resorption and deposition — resorption dominating in early stages, then disorganised new bone laid down in its place [1]. The jaws are affected alongside the skull, pelvis, and long bones: the maxilla more often than the mandible [2]. As the bone enlarges and deforms, dentures that previously fitted become increasingly ill-fitting and eventually unwearable, because the arch dimensions have changed.

Hypercementosis — thickening of the cementum layer around tooth roots — is a direct consequence of the same disordered bone-cementum metabolism [2]. The root becomes fused or adhered to the surrounding bone in a way that makes extraction extremely difficult. This is the relevant clinical trap: what looks like a routine extraction is not.
problems.presentation:
- Patient over 55 with existing complete or partial dentures that have progressively stopped fitting, without the usual explanation of ridge resorption.
- Jaw pain and possible cranial nerve symptoms if the skull base is involved [1].
- On examination: the jaws may appear enlarged, the palatal vault flattened or expanded, the dental arches widened.
- The patient may report that recent extractions elsewhere were unexpectedly difficult.
- Systemic features: bone pain elsewhere, skull changes, hearing loss if auditory nerve compressed.
problems.results:
- **Radiograph**: characteristic 'cotton wool' appearance of affected bone — patchy sclerosis mixed with areas of radiolucency, giving an irregular mottled pattern [2]. Loss of the normal trabecular architecture.
- **Bloods**: raised serum alkaline phosphatase and raised urinary hydroxyproline are the biochemical hallmarks [2]. These reflect the high rate of bone turnover.
- DPT confirms hypercementosis around roots of standing teeth: the root outline is bulbous and the periodontal ligament space may be obliterated in places.
- The combination of jaw enlargement, cotton wool radiographic appearance, and elevated alkaline phosphatase is effectively diagnostic.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The question to ask when dentures keep failing without the usual ridge resorption pattern is: is the jaw actually getting bigger rather than smaller? Paget's is the condition where the bone expands rather than resorbs — the opposite mechanism to the usual denture failure story [1].

The interesting bit from a prosthetic standpoint is the double risk: not only do dentures fail because the arch dimensions change, but any extraction needed to improve the denture-bearing area carries a disproportionate BRONJ risk. Paget's disease is a standard indication for bisphosphonate therapy, and once the patient is on bisphosphonates, jaw surgery carries a risk of osteonecrosis ranging from under 1% for low-potency oral preparations up to 30% for patients on IV preparations who have had extractions [3].
problems.treatment:
- Manage ill-fitting dentures conservatively wherever possible: reline, rebase, or remake rather than extracting standing teeth.
- Before any surgical procedure including extraction: check whether the patient is on bisphosphonates or calcitonin for Paget's disease [2]. If so, apply BRONJ precautions — prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic technique, primary closure over bone to prevent necrosis [4].
- Avoid general anaesthesia where possible [2].
- Hypercementosis means roots are difficult to remove: extraction should be planned surgically rather than with a simple forceps technique [2].
- For established BRONJ if it develops: refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery — there are no agreed effective treatments and local sequestrectomy with coverage is the best available approach [4].
- The systemic disease is managed with bisphosphonates and calcitonin [2]; the GDP's role is to coordinate dental treatment around that.
problems.prognosis: The bony enlargement in Paget's is progressive during the active phase of the disease. Bisphosphonates stabilise the process but do not reverse existing jaw changes, so dentures will remain a persistent management problem. Hypercementosis does not resolve. If BRONJ develops, the condition appears to be progressive and there is no established effective treatment [3].

citations.quote: A common disorder of the elderly, where the normal, orderly replacement of bone is disrupted and replaced by a chaotic structure of new bone, causing enlargement and deformity. The hands and feet are spared. Complications include bone pain and cranial nerve compression, or, more rarely, high output cardiac failure or osteosarcoma. Another condition that is treated with bisphosphonates.

This is relatively common over the age of 55yrs and affects the skull, pelvis, and long bones, as well as the jaws. Although aetiology is uncertain, both the measles and respiratory syncytial viruses have been implicated. The maxilla is more frequently affected than the mandible. Hypercementosis of roots makes extractions difficult in this group. There is a replacement of normal bone remodelling by a chaotic alternation of resorption and deposition, with resorption dominating in the early stages. Bone pain and cranial neuropathies can occur. X-rays show a 'cotton wool' appearance. Biochemistry shows an ↑ in alkaline phosphatase and urinary hydroxyproline. Avoid GA; use prophylactic antibiotics and plan extractions surgically. Bisphosphonates and calcitonin are used in Rx.

Bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (BRONJ aka BRON aka anti-resorptive-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (ARONJ)) is a condition where alveolar bone is exposed in the mouth in patients taking these drugs (Fig. 10.2). The condition appears to be progressive and there is no established effective treatment although several are being investigated. Bone necrosis without mucosal breach is also described. The incidence is variable but is probably much less than 1% for patients treated with low-potency drugs for osteoporosis, up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10yrs who have received highly potent drugs and who have had extractions.

There will be many instances where patients have been started on these drugs and need teeth removed. If this can be avoided by endodontics, coronectomy, etc. then do it. If not, warn the patient of risks (range from <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis patient to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10yrs). Use prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, and alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone lies well below the gingival margin and close mucosa primarily.
